item.title: Setting Up a Test About Mean Ambulance Response Time
item.stimulus: A city's emergency services department states that the mean response time for ambulance calls is 8.0 minutes. A resident believes the true mean response time is longer. The resident obtains the department's records of about 5,400 calls from the past year and takes a simple random sample of 36 of those calls. The sample mean response time is 8.7 minutes and the sample standard deviation is 2.9 minutes. The distribution of the 36 response times is skewed to the right, with no extreme outliers.

parts.prompt: State the null and alternative hypotheses for a test of the resident's belief, defining any parameter you use.

criteria.text: Defines μ as the true mean response time (in minutes) for all ambulance calls in the city.
criteria.evidence: Response defines the parameter as a population mean in context, with the population of ambulance calls and units of minutes.
criteria.fix: Define the parameter in words: name it as a population mean and say which population it describes, with units.

criteria.text: States the null hypothesis H0: μ = 8.0 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Response writes H0 with equality and the claimed value 8.0.
criteria.fix: Write H0 as the parameter equal to the value claimed by the department, 8.0 minutes.

criteria.text: States the alternative hypothesis Ha: μ > 8.0 minutes.
criteria.evidence: Response writes Ha with the greater-than sign, reflecting the resident's belief that the mean is longer.
criteria.fix: Match the direction of Ha to the belief: longer than 8.0 minutes means the parameter is greater than 8.0.

parts.prompt: Name the inference procedure that is appropriate for these hypotheses.

criteria.text: Identifies a one-sample t-test for a population mean.
criteria.evidence: Response names a one-sample t-test (or t-test for a mean), not a z-test and not a two-sample test.
criteria.fix: One quantitative variable from one sample with unknown population standard deviation calls for a one-sample t-test for a mean.

parts.prompt: Verify the conditions for using this procedure.

criteria.text: Verifies the random condition and the 10% condition: the calls are a simple random sample, and 5,400 is more than 10 × 36 = 360.
criteria.evidence: Response states that the sample is random and compares the population of about 5,400 calls with 10 times the sample size, 360.
criteria.fix: State how the sample was selected and compare the population size with 10 times the sample size.

criteria.text: Verifies the sample data condition: n = 36 is at least 30, so the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even though the sample is skewed to the right.
criteria.evidence: Response states that n ≥ 30 justifies approximate normality of the sampling distribution despite skewness.
criteria.fix: Compare n with 30; when n is at least 30, skewness in the sample does not stop you from using t procedures.

item.model_answer:
(a) Let μ be the true mean response time, in minutes, for all ambulance calls in the city. H0: μ = 8.0 minutes. Ha: μ > 8.0 minutes.

(b) A one-sample t-test for a population mean is appropriate.

(c) Random: the 36 calls are a simple random sample. 10%: there are about 5,400 calls, which is more than 10 × 36 = 360. Sample data: n = 36 is at least 30, so the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal even though the sample is skewed to the right.
